title-group.article-title: Efficacy and safety of frameless versus frame-based stereotactic biopsy for brainstem lesions: A comparison demonstrating comparable outcomes with frameless technique

sec.title: Background:
sec.p: The brainstem tumors are rare and extremely heterogeneous, presenting significant challenges in the surgical approach. For lesions that are not candidates for surgical resection, a definitive diagnosis is primarily obtained through stereotactic biopsy. However, the diagnostic yield, safety, and complication rate of frameless stereotactic techniques are still subject of debates in the literature, especially in eloquent or deep regions such as the brainstem. The aim of this study is to demonstrate that the frameless technique can achieve similar results to the frame-based technique, by comparing the results of the both techniques, even in critical regions, such as the brainstem.

sec.title: Methods:
sec.p: Twenty-nine frame-based stereotactic biopsies and 17 frameless biopsies of brainstem lesions were analyzed. Diagnostic confirmation of the lesions was performed through histopathological and immunohistochemical analysis and compared between the two groups of patients. The Statistical Package for the Social Science (IBM® Statistical Package for the Social Sciences) software was used for statistical analysis, testing normality between groups with the Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Fisher’s tests to assess the association of the use of each technique in the diagnosis, the complication rate and mortality, in addition to assessing whether the was a correlation between the effectiveness of the methods and the age group, gender, approaches, Karnofsky performance scale, location of the tumors, contrast-enhancing in images, with a 95% confidence interval.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Furthermore, it was observed that the only factor studied that increased the efficacy rate was the use of the transfrontal route, with an overall efficacy rate of 78.3% (36 patients) and P = 0.001.

sec.title: Conclusion:
sec.p: The frameless and frame-based stereotactic techniques not show statistically significant differences in terms of diagnostic yield, complications rates and mortality. Both can be used depending on the availability and experience of the service, offering flexibility in choosing the approach for biopsy of brainstem lesions.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: The brainstem tumors are rare and extremely heterogeneous, presenting significant challenges in surgical management. Definitive diagnosis of brainstem lesions that are not candidates for surgical resection is obtained mainly through stereotactic biopsies.[2]

The frame-based technique is considered the gold standard for biopsy of posterior fossa tumors, including the brainstem and cerebellum, due to its high accuracy and stability. These systems have demonstrated diagnostic success rates of 80–95%, specially in lesions located in eloquent regions, such as the brainstem, offering high safety and reliability.[6,9] Although the frame-based approach is widely used and established, it may have limitations in patients with challenging anatomical conditions, such as short neck or kyphosis, and in children, which makes adequate positioning of the stereotactic halo difficult.[9]

On the other hand, frameless techniques have gained increasing popularity due to their flexibility, shorter procedure time and ability to adapt to different anatomies. However, the diagnostic efficacy and safety of the frameless stereotactic technique are still debated in the literature.[3,19]
Through comparative analysis of the results of both techniques, the study aims to determine the feasibility and reliability of the frameless method as an alternative for biopsy of brainstem lesions.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This is a retrospective observational study conducted in the Neurosurgery Department of Santa Casa of Belo Horizonte (Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais, Brazil). The study followed internationally accepted ethical parameters, and the study was approved by the Institution’s Research Ethics Committee. The Institutional Research and Medical Ethics Committee granted ethical (CAAE 48198721.7.0000.5138) and all participants provided informed consent. It is reported following the Preferred Reporting of Case Series in Surgery Guidelines.

sec.title: Study population
sec.p: This study included 46 patients with brainstem lesions on preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The patients were divided into two groups, with 29 patients undergoing frame-based stereotactic biopsy and 17 patients undergoing frameless biopsy.

sec.title: Data collection
sec.p: Data were collected by reviewing the medical records of patients who underwent biopsy between January 2019 and May 2024.

sec.title: Frameless surgical technique
sec.p: The frameless stereotactic-guided biopsies were planned based on MRI images in T1-weighted with gadolinium, T2 and T2 Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR), acquired with axial slices of 1 mm thickness. The images were co-registered and the surgical planning of the target and trajectory of the procedures was performed on a StealthStation S7® neuronavigation station (Medtronic®, Minneapolis, USA), with the aid of Cranial® software version 5.0 (Medtronic®, Minneapolis, USA). The Medtronic® Navigus Frameless Brain Biopsy Kit was used. The surgeries were performed under general anesthesia, with small linear incisions in the scalp and a single cranial trepanation, with a length of 10 mm. The fragments were collected and sent for histopathological analysis.

sec.title: Frame-based surgical technique
sec.p: In patients undergoing frame-based stereotactic guided biopsy, the Cosman-Roberts-Wells (CRW) halo (Integra LifeSciences Corporation, Princeton, NJ, USA) was used. The stereotactic halo was implanted under local anesthesia, and the patient underwent a cranial computed tomography scan with 1-mm slices and 9 fiducials for surgical planning. After the examination, the image was transferred to the Medtronic StealthStation S7 neuronavigation device. Planning was performed using x, y, z, arc, and ring coordinates to propose the trajectory. The procedure was performed under sedation and local anesthesia. After planning the coordinates, a linear incision was made in the skin followed by trepanation. The fragments were collected and sent for histopathological analysis.

sec.title: Data analysis
sec.p: The diagnostic confirmation of the lesions was performed through histopathological and immunohistochemical analysis, comparing the results between the two groups of patients. The Statistical Package for the Social Sciences IBM® software was used for statistical analysis, testing normality between the groups with the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. In addition, the independent variable (treatment modality) was evaluated regarding age group, gender, access routes, Karnofsky performance scale (KPS), tumor location, and contrast uptake using the Chi-square test. A difference was identified between the groups regarding the approach route. Therefore, to control for this possible confounding factor, an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) was performed to assess the association of the use of each technique with the diagnostic and complication rates. In all tests, P < 0.05 was considered significant. The route for approach was chosen according to the basic principles of brain biopsy: Shorter route, avoiding eloquent area, entry point in cortical gyrus, and avoiding passage through deep vessels and ventricle.

sec.title: Clinical-epidemiological characteristics
sec.p: A total of 46 patients were evaluated, comprising 27 males (58.7%) and 19 females (41.3%). The mean age of the patients was 30 years, with ages ranging from 3 to 75 years.

The transfrontal approach was performed in 36 patients (78.2%), while the suboccipital approach was used in 10 cases (21.8%). Most lesions were solitary, with the pons being the most commonly affected region. Regarding patient functionality in the preoperative period, the majority were clinically stable and able to perform basic daily activities. Forty patients (87%) had a KPS score above 70%, whereas 6 patients (13%) were already significantly compromised by the underlying disease [Table 1]. The analysis of the studied variables between groups showed a statistically significant difference only in the surgical approach, with the suboccipital approach being more frequent in the frameless group – likely due to its greater feasibility compared to the frame-based group [Table 2].

Clinical-epidemiological table between the different surgical techniques.

sec.p: Regarding this difference between the approach modalities, ANCOVA was used to evaluate the association between the use of each approach and the diagnostic and complication rates. Thus, it revealed that there is no effect of the access covariate on the diagnostic rate (F [1.43] = 0.01; P = 0.803) and on the complication rate (F (1.43) = 0.195; P = 0.226).

sec.title: Frame-based technique biopsy group
sec.p: From January 2020 to December 2021, a total of 29 stereotactic brainstem biopsies were performed and recorded using the frame-based technique using the Hallo CRW. Of these, 18 patients were male (62%) and 11 were female (38%) [Table 2].

sec.title: Frameless technique biopsy group
sec.p: Data were collected prospectively between December 2023 and May 2024, with a total of 17 biopsies recorded with the frameless technique. Of these, 10 patients were male (58.8%) and 7 were female (41.2%) [Table 2].

sec.title: Overall
sec.p: The overall diagnostic rate was 38 patients (82.6%), mostly high- and low-grade gliomas. It was observed that 7 patients (15.2%) developed complications, and of these, 2 patients (11.8%) died [Table 1].

sec.title: Frame-based technique
sec.p: The diagnosis was confirmed in 24 cases (82.8%). As for complications, these were present in 3 patients (10.3%) in the frame-based group. One patient presented worsening of the paresis of the third cranial nerve, but with recovery of the deficit; in another case, bleeding from the surgical bed was evidenced with worsening of the previous facial paresis; and a final patient presented severe hemiparesis in the immediate postoperative period, and these last two did not recover the motor deficits acquired with the procedure [Table 3].

caption.p: Rate of complications and deaths of the frame-based technique.

sec.title: Frameless technique
sec.p: The diagnosis was conclusive in 14 patients (82.4%), and inconclusive in 3 patients (17.6%). Complications occurred in 4 patients (23.5%) in the frameless group. Worsening of the motor deficit with recovery was observed in two patients (11.8%), sensory impairment due to cerebral edema and herniation was observed in another, requiring decompressive craniectomy, and one patient developed bacterial meningitis, with these last two patients dying [Table 4].

caption.p: Rate of complications and deaths of the frameless technique.

sec.title: Frame-based versus frameless technique
sec.p: When comparing the diagnostic rate between the two techniques, the Chi-square test was performed to assess efficacy, and P-value was 0.972, that is, there was no statistical significance between the techniques [Table 5].

caption.p: Efficacy and safety of frameless and frame-based stereotactic biopsies.

sec.p: Analyzing complications, permanent neurological deficits were observed in 2 patients (11.8%) in the frameless group and in 2 patients (6.8%) in the frame-based group. However, this difference was not statistically significant (P = 0.229).
As for mortality, 2 patients (11.8%) died in the frameless technique, and there were no deaths in the frame-based technique; however, there was also no statistical significance, P = 0.059.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: Brainstem tumors represent approximately 10% of all central nervous system (CNS) tumors, with gliomas and primary CNS lymphoma being the most common types. In lesions where microsurgical resection is not indicated, stereotactic biopsy represents a fundamental step in the diagnosis and definition of the therapeutic approach.[5,7]

The gold standard for stereotactic biopsy is the frame-based technique, which demonstrates good results. The study by Hirano et al., with 22 patients during the years 2002–2021, undergoing frame-based stereotactic biopsy, elucidated a diagnostic rate of around 95%, and a morbidity rate of 0.5–3% for permanent deficits or major complications.[7]

Li et al. [11] also used the frame-based stereotaxic technique in a study with 11 patients and obtained a diagnostic rate of 90.9%. Two patients presented neurological deficits but recovered within 3 months. Dellaretti et al., in a study in 2009 with 80 patients between 1984 and 2007, obtained a diagnostic rate of around 96.3%, with gliomas being the predominant histopathological finding. In the study by Kaes et al. with 79 cases submitted to frame-based biopsy, a diagnostic rate of 87.3% (69 patients) and an overall morbidity of 8.9% were observed, with hemorrhage being evidenced in five cases that presented complications, of which four had temporary deficits and three permanent deficits. Mortality within 30 days after biopsy was 6 cases (7.6%).[2,9,11]

In the study by Quick-Weller et al., 26 patients underwent frameless biopsy, with a diagnosis obtained in 100% of patients and 19.2% of patients presenting complications, including one case of facial paralysis, one hydrocephalus, and three cases with minor bleeding in the biopsy area. Mortality was 3.8%; one patient developed hydrocephalus due to mesencephalic edema and another presented pneumonia as a secondary complication to neurological worsening, culminating in death a few days after the procedure, however, he already presented an unfavorable clinical condition with a KPS of 50.[16]

In the present study, 29 patients underwent the frame-based technique, achieving a diagnostic rate of approximately 90%, compatible with the values reported in the literature. Complication rates also showed similar rates to those described in previous studies.[12]

Despite the good results, and the frame-based approach being widely used and established, it may present limitations in patients with challenging anatomical conditions, such as short neck or kyphosis, and in children, which makes it difficult to position the stereotactic halo properly. In addition, this method may involve a long procedure time and anesthesia. Thus, the frameless technique has been gaining popularity due to its flexibility, shorter procedure time, and ability to adapt to different anatomies.[4]

In the frameless technique, imaging examination and surgical planning can be performed in advance. The fiducials are marked after anesthetic induction, thus reducing surgical time, as evidenced in some studies such as that of Li et al., who retrospectively studied 33 patients, with an average time of 84.7 min in the frameless technique and a diagnostic rate of 95.5%, and in the frame-based technique of 124.5 min with a diagnostic rate of 90.9%, also providing greater comfort to the patient and effectiveness to the surgical procedure.[11,13]

Peciu-Florianu et al. demonstrated diagnostic rates of 95.8% in 96 patients, with complication rates of 19.4% in total, including permanent deficits in 3 cases (2.9%) and transient deficits with complete recovery in 17.7% of cases. In this study, we observed one death due to intratumoral hematoma and compression of adjacent structures.[14] In the clinical trial by Kreatsoulas et al., a diagnostic rate of 100% and 7.2% of complications were observed.[10] Anton Fruh et al.[3] found a diagnostic rate of 97% in 12 pediatric patients who underwent biopsy using the frameless technique, with no permanent deficits reported in these patients and no deaths. All these studies corroborate the data found in the present study, which obtained a diagnostic rate with the frameless technique of 82.4%, with two patients presenting permanent neurological deficits and two deaths, one due to edema in the brainstem after biopsy and the other due to meningitis.[8,17,18]

As demonstrated, we found several publications addressing the use of frame-based and frameless techniques for brainstem tumors; however, to date, there are no direct comparative studies between these approaches, highlighting the importance of this investigation.[13]

When comparing the efficacy and safety between the two groups of patients, we found no statistically significant difference in relation to the diagnostic rate and complications. These findings suggest that the frameless technique, even in eloquent areas, may be a viable and safe alternative, offering additional benefits, such as greater flexibility and shorter procedure time. Thus, this study contributes to the understanding of the options available for biopsy of brainstem lesions and reinforces the possibility of choosing the technique based on the available resources and the team’s experience.[1,15,20]

sec.title: Limitations of the study
sec.p: It is important to recognize that the comparative results between these techniques may be influenced by factors such as the number of patients, the experience of the surgical team in each technique, and variations in the navigation systems used. In addition, this is a single-center, retrospective study.

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: This study demonstrated that frameless and frame-based techniques for stereotactic brainstem biopsies have comparable efficacy and safety. Therefore, both can be used according to the availability of resources and the experience of the team. These findings reinforce the feasibility of both approaches and contribute to clinical decision-making, allowing greater flexibility in the choice of technique based on the specific conditions of each neurosurgery service.
